title: the product: installation, server and documentation for a person
intent: Parity from the point of view of a person includes the parts that are not the kernel: how the harness is installed, how it is served, and how it is explained to someone who is not reading its source. The reference harnesses spend most of their code there. This wave is the product layer, and it is also where the strongest objection to the whole architecture is settled: an agent on a phone, running the same task through Emacs Lisp and through shell, where the Emacs arm needs a package manager and the shell arm does not.
objection: The bootstrap is the part that does not travel, and the installation is where it shows: a package manager on a phone is a worse user experience than a shell that is already there.
refuted_by: The same task through Emacs Lisp and through shell on a phone, with the Emacs arm needing a package manager. If that is the bottleneck every time, the architecture is wrong and the kernel should not have been Elisp.
note: The session is written for the machine and exported for the person: `M-x yeah-export' writes the journal as an Org file, one heading per event, with the text of the event in a block that Org cannot mistake for syntax. The live coding task is checked against a real provider (MiniMax-M2.7): the harness reads the project, edits the file with a guarded edit, saves it and the test passes. The interactive UI path is not tested.
